content: Weather maps of distant planets are a step closer after the James Webb Space Telescope distinguished hotter and cooler regions around the giant exoplanet WASP-17b. One side of WASP-17b’s atmosphere extends farther into space than the other, giving this intensely hot giant planet an uneven outline. Astronomers have now mapped that distortion with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), finding a pattern consistent with predictions of how heat and powerful winds shape a world with permanent day and night sides. WASP-17b is a hot Jupiter, a giant planet that orbits close to its star, about 1,300 light-years from Earth. The study, co-led by Cornell University in the United States and the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom, was published in Nature Astronomy . It marks the first application of a method called transmission strings, developed at Bristol by astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford. “Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds,” said Wakeford, a study co-author and associate professor of astrophysics at the University of Bristol. JWST, the largest telescope in space, has already enabled researchers to use a technique called eclipse mapping, which measures changes in light as a planet passes behind its host star. Transmission strings, also called transit mapping, follows the planet as it crosses in front of the star. It analyzes the light passing through different parts of the atmosphere’s edge, or limb, to distinguish conditions around that boundary. Traditional modeling instead extracts a single spectrum, a measurement of light across different wavelengths, averaged over the entire limb. Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell, began the investigation at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics. “Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet,” Alderson said. “We’re able to go around the edge. So, we’ve gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak.” On WASP-17b, the mapped bulge lies on the evening side of the equator. There, jets of wind carry heat from the permanently illuminated day side toward the permanently shadowed night side, inflating the atmosphere relative to the equator’s cooler morning side. The location matches what theory and previous modeling had indicated. “Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend – pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be,” Alderson said. The study’s findings on atmospheric chemical composition and temperature differences, both from equator to poles and between the day and night sides, also agree with theoretical predictions and other modeling techniques. “Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting,” Wakeford said. Together, the findings provide one of the most comprehensive three-dimensional views of an exoplanet’s atmosphere. They also establish a benchmark for comparison with the more than 6,000 other exoplanets confirmed to date. “This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter,” Alderson said. The successful demonstration on WASP-17b opens the way to applying transmission strings to many more planets. The method is beginning to distinguish conditions across different latitudes, extending atmospheric maps beyond the contrast between day and night. That is a first step toward mapping weather-scale patterns in exoplanet climates. Reference: “A spatial map of the atmospheric limb of a hot Jupiter” by Lili Alderson, Hannah R. Wakeford, David Grant, Nikole K. Lewis, Avinash Verma, Jayesh Goyal, Mark Hammond, Daniel Valentine, Natalie H. Allen, Ana Glidden, Amélie Gressier, Jingcheng Huang, Maura Lally, Dana R. Louie, Jacob Lustig-Yaeger, Cathal Maguire, Elijah Mullens, Kristin S. Sotzen, Jeff A. Valenti, Roeland P. van der Marel and Tiffany Kataria, 14 October 2026, Nature Astronomy . DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02986-4 Funding is provided to the team by NASA through grant number 80NSSC20K0586. Based on observations with the NASA/ESA/CSA JWST, associated with program(s) GTO-1353 (PI: N.K.L.), obtained at the Space Telescope Science Institute, which is operated by AURA, Inc., under NASA contract NAS 5-03127. content: Curiosity’s latest panorama sharpens the view of a Martian rock layer that looks out of place and may have formed from ancient volcanic ash. A band of wind-carved cliffs stretches roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp on Mars, and NASA’s Curiosity rover is climbing toward it. A newly released panorama offers the most detailed view yet of these formations, known as yardangs, which mission scientists have long wanted to examine up close. “The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.” Curiosity has been ascending the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain since 2014. Each layer records a different period in Mars’ history, allowing scientists to reconstruct a time billions of years ago when lakes and streams covered this region . As the water dried up, it left salty minerals behind. Once new material stopped accumulating on the mountain, wind may have stripped some of it away to create the yardangs. The panorama captures the distant cliffs in bright morning light, with blue hues across the foreground. Curiosity’s Mastcam took the six images that make up the scene at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time on Aug. 11, the mission’s 4,982nd Martian day, or sol. The images were transmitted to Earth and stitched together. Unlike most Mastcam imagery, the panorama was processed without the color adjustment known as white balancing, preserving its early morning appearance. The rover recently reached another milestone in its ascent, gaining 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars. It is now in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which began with an exploration of spiderweb-like formations called boxwork ridges. For most of the next year or so, Curiosity will drive through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying at the surface. Scientists expect increasingly detailed images as the rover approaches the cliffs. They hope to reach the base of the yardangs sometime in 2027, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect unique data about the formations and investigate how they came to be. title: Women may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why
content: Decades before Siri or Alexa or ChatGPT, there was a real person, almost always a woman, at the center of the information world. She was so vital, most long-distance communication could not happen without her. She was the telephone switch operator, and at one time she was part of the single largest occupation for white, U.S.-born women under age 20. Today, that job doesn't exist. The world is struggling to figure out what the dawn of artificial intelligence means for society, culture and the economy. A lot of ordinary Americans are just wondering what it means for their jobs. The history of technological progress — from automated telephone switches to the introduction of the washing machine and the personal computer — can offer some guidance. And that guidance suggests women are likely to be among the most affected by AI. "AI is focused on routine tasks and numbers and finding patterns, and those types of jobs are the clerical, administrative jobs that a lot of women hold,'' said Ariane Hegewisch, a senior research fellow at the Institute for Women's Policy Research. "It's still 90% of secretaries and clerical workers who are women." New research backs this up. The International Labour Organization in March concluded that nearly 1 in 10 women in high-income countries work in occupations at the highest risk from AI. In the 1940s, nearly 95% of America's telephone operators were female. It was a relatively well-paying job for women at the time, and a complicated one: It took months of training to be able to handle the several hundred calls an hour that could come in at peak times. Operators were expected to be speedy, precise — and polite. These women were hit hard when AT&T introduced the automated telephone switch. It was one of the largest automation investments in history — a close analog to the massive AI investment now underway — and created one of the biggest technological shocks the nation had ever seen. In the decades after the automated switch was popularized, an estimated 75,000 operator jobs vanished. Economists James Feigenbaum at Boston University and Daniel P. Gross at Duke University's Fuqua School of Business studied census and paycheck data from the time and followed local employment trends along the path of AT&T's rolling investment in switches across the nation. "The effect of this shock on incumbent operators was to dispossess many of their jobs and careers," they wrote in 2020 . Many switchboard operators wound up in lower-paying jobs — or dropped out of the workforce entirely, they found. Economist David Autor said this outcome reflects the reality that many workers are already in their highest and best-paying occupation. When the job goes away, the next step is often down. "Most people are not changing careers very often. They make their career decisions early, and they stick with those careers," he said. "If those careers, if the value of that work ... suddenly goes out of fashion, becomes technologically obsolete, they're going to, in general, do something not as good." But Feigenbaum and Gross also discovered that the next generation of women fared better. "Future workers found work in other fields, often taking up similar-quality jobs," they wrote, as the younger workers were "more adaptive to an evolving labor market ... Anxiety over the opportunities available to future generations proved to be somewhat misplaced." In other words: One type of job went away, but other work emerged over time that was just as good. By the 1950s, another technological innovation would come along and have a profound effect on women: the washing machine. Dubbed " engines of liberation " in a seminal paper on the topic by University of Pennsylvania economist Jeremy Greenwood and others, washing machines and other appliances dramatically reduced the time women spent on unpaid housework. That meant time could be reallocated to a paycheck outside the home, even as women's responsibility for the home remained. From 1950 to 1980, as gender norms changed, the number of employed women in the U.S. grew by more than 25 million. Their participation rate, or share of the female population in the labor force, grew to 52% from 34%. At the same time, 16 million more men found work, though the male participation rate dropped by 5 percentage points. The relevant question for the AI boom today: How did the economy suddenly find jobs for these women? If AI creates a vast new pool of available workers, can the economy put them to work? First, the very entry of women into the workforce meant demand for tasks once done at home moved into the paid economy, services such as childcare and food preparation. Second, as the nation grew wealthier, other employment opportunities for women emerged in the service economy — in retail, restaurants, leisure and hospitality, and even some professional services . And third, as American businesses grew, they needed more people to handle the paperwork — everything from payroll to customer accounts. Changes to the economy and businesses were partly related to the entry of women into the workforce, but it was also partly random luck that the U.S. was booming and businesses were changing to need more office workers. "Between 1940 and 1980, there was a ton of new work created in the U.S. economy, and it was in office and clerical work that was accessible to people with a high school education,'' Autor said. The next big revolution affecting women in the workplace was the personal computer. Before PCs arrived on the scene, women were the backbone of office infrastructure. According to the 1980 U.S. census, nearly 4.7 million Americans worked as secretaries, stenographers and typists. More than 98% were women. When IBM introduced the personal computer in 1981, followed by the advent of Microsoft Word just two years later, some of the middlemen, or in this case, middlewomen, became obsolete. It didn't eliminate writing, filing or editing. It simply shifted a big chunk of those tasks from dedicated clerical workers to others in the office — executives could type their own reports, book their own travel and print their own papers. But the PC wasn't entirely bad news for women in the workforce. Studies show women were already more likely than men to be using a computer at work at the dawn of the PC era. The PC put new tools at their fingertips: spreadsheets and databases and general computing power. While many roles were eliminated, many women adapted and found new ways to use the emerging technology to make themselves indispensable to their employers. That's a potential outcome for AI. In some cases, it will eliminate tasks but not entire jobs, enhancing the time and ability of a worker to do the remaining value-added jobs that only humans can do. A 2022 paper by Marcus Dillender and Eliza Forsythe found that when companies adopted software to do office and administrative work, it resulted in a 1% decline in employment in the sector but a 3% increase in wages for college graduates. Many more women have earned college and advanced degrees, and hold managerial jobs, than when other technologies ripped through the economy, offering some potential protection from automation. But maybe not for long: One of the promises of AI is that it will move up the value chain of the jobs performed by humans. Whatever capabilities the new technology may have now, the outlook is unclear because, Hegewisch says, somewhat ominously, "AI can learn."
ranking_reason: AI's focus on routine tasks and numbers, and its ability to find patterns, suggests women are likely to be among the most affected by AI.

The inclusion of expert quotes and data from reputable sources, such as the International Labour Organization, supports the claim that women are likely to be affected by AI. This article provides a clear reason for readers to care, as it explores a timely and relevant topic with significant implications for the workforce.
